messages.content: I want to develop a legged locomotion controller that identifies hidden terrain yielding limits while maintaining recoverability during exploratory foot contacts. What are the central aims?

There are two linked aims: learn how much load previously unseen terrain can bear, and keep the robot able to recover while its foot contacts explore that terrain. Exploration should contribute information about a hidden yielding limit without treating a potentially yielding contact as though its capacity were already known.
Can you make the performance requirements explicit?

The controller should estimate previously unseen terrain’s load-bearing limits with a median relative error below 15%. It should also reduce falls by 30% compared with an otherwise matched nonexploratory controller, with the two compared at equal traversal speed. These are targets for the controller, not reported results.
What does “hidden terrain yielding limits” mean here?

It refers to limits on what the terrain can bear before it yields, where those limits are not known to the controller in advance. The development goal is for the controller to identify those limits through its interactions with previously unseen terrain. The statement does not specify a terrain type or a particular way to measure or infer a limit.
And why emphasize recoverability during exploratory foot contacts?

An exploratory contact is meant to reveal something about uncertain support. Recoverability adds the constraint that seeking that information should not leave the robot unable to respond if the support proves insufficient. The goal joins information gathering and continued control; it does not define a particular recovery maneuver.
So should I describe the controller as probing the terrain aggressively until it finds the exact point of failure?

That would go beyond the stated goal. It calls for identifying yielding limits while maintaining recoverability during exploratory foot contacts. It does not prescribe aggressive probing, require inducing failure, or specify an exact point-finding procedure.
How should I read “median relative error below 15%”? Is it a guarantee for every estimate?

No. A median requirement concerns the middle of the collection of relative errors used in an evaluation; it does not, by itself, bound every individual error. The target is specifically below 15% for estimates of previously unseen terrain’s load-bearing limits. The statement does not supply an evaluation dataset or a more detailed error protocol.
Does “previously unseen” matter, or is the estimation target just about terrain the controller already knows?

It matters. The target is estimation on previously unseen terrain, so the intended capability is not merely recalling a known load-bearing limit. That wording does not specify how different the unseen terrain may be from any terrain encountered before.
Explain the falls comparison without adding assumptions about the baseline.

The comparison is against an otherwise matched nonexploratory controller at equal traversal speed. The target is a 30% reduction in falls relative to that comparator. “Otherwise matched” and “equal traversal speed” are important conditions: the fall reduction should not be framed as a comparison to a differently matched controller or one moving at a different speed.
Does the 30% reduction say what traversal speed to use?

No. It specifies that traversal speed must be equal in the comparison, but it does not name a speed. Likewise, it does not specify the terrain, trial count, or precise fall-reporting procedure for that comparison.
Could the controller meet the aim just by avoiding exploratory contacts altogether?

That would omit an essential part of the goal. The controller is meant to identify hidden yielding limits during exploratory foot contacts while maintaining recoverability. Avoiding all such contacts would not express the stated exploratory identification objective, even if it avoided some immediate contact risks.
What if it learns the limits well but falls more often than the nonexploratory controller?

Good estimation alone would not satisfy both stated requirements. The goal pairs a median relative estimation error below 15% with 30% fewer falls than an otherwise matched nonexploratory controller at equal traversal speed. Neither target replaces the other.
Conversely, is a lower fall rate enough if the controller cannot estimate the yielding limits accurately?

No. The fall comparison addresses safety during traversal, while the estimation threshold addresses identification of load-bearing limits on previously unseen terrain. The controller is intended to meet both, alongside the broader aim of maintaining recoverability during exploratory contacts.
Is recoverability itself assigned a numerical threshold?

Not in this statement. Maintaining recoverability is part of the controller’s goal during exploratory foot contacts, but no separate numerical recoverability metric or threshold is given. The explicit numerical requirements are median relative error below 15% and a 30% fall reduction under the specified comparison.
Then give me a concise formulation that keeps all of the conditions intact.

Develop a legged locomotion controller that uses exploratory foot contacts to identify hidden yielding limits on previously unseen terrain while maintaining recoverability. It should estimate that terrain’s load-bearing limits with median relative error below 15% and reduce falls by 30% versus an otherwise matched nonexploratory controller at equal traversal speed.
How could we pursue the terrain-identification goal without losing the ability to recover during exploratory contacts?

The proposed approach combines graded-load foot probes with Bayesian force–sinkage inference to estimate yield limits. Alongside that, viability-constrained model predictive control (MPC) would reserve recovery steps. The first part addresses what can be learned from a contact; the second keeps recovery available while those contacts are planned.
What makes a foot probe “graded-load”?

It means applying load in grades rather than treating the exploratory contact as a single, all-at-once loading event. The resulting observations can inform an estimate of how the terrain responds as load changes. The proposal does not specify the number of grades, their magnitudes, or a loading schedule.
Is the probe supposed to push the foot until the ground gives way?

Not necessarily. The proposal is to use graded-load probes to help estimate a yield limit, while reserving recovery steps. It does not require deliberately reaching failure on every probe or prescribe how far any individual contact should be taken.
What information does “force–sinkage” refer to?

It refers to the relationship between the force applied through a foot contact and how much the foot sinks into the terrain. Changes in that relationship can be informative about load-bearing behavior. The proposal names this relationship as the basis for inference, without specifying an exact force–sinkage model.
Why call the inference Bayesian?

Bayesian inference represents uncertainty about the yield limit and updates that uncertainty in light of observations from the probes. That is useful when the limit is hidden and a contact provides incomplete information. The proposal does not fix a prior, likelihood, or particular update method.
So is each probe expected to produce a certain answer about the limit?

No. A probe may narrow or shift an uncertain estimate, but the proposal does not say that any one contact identifies the limit with certainty. Bayesian force–sinkage inference is a way to reason from the available contact observations while retaining uncertainty.
How does viability-constrained MPC fit beside that estimation process?

The inference concerns what the terrain may bear; viability-constrained MPC concerns what actions the controller can plan while keeping recovery possible. In this proposal, the MPC component reserves recovery steps as exploratory contacts are considered. It is the planning counterpart to the graded-load probing and yield-limit estimation.
What does it mean to reserve a recovery step? Does the robot have to take one after every probe?

Reserving recovery steps means leaving recovery options available in the plan if an exploratory contact does not provide the support expected. It does not mean taking a recovery step after every probe. The proposal also does not specify a fixed number of reserved steps or their locations.
Could we describe the MPC constraint as a guarantee that no fall can occur?

That would overstate it. A viability constraint expresses the planning aim of retaining recoverable options, but the proposal does not claim an absolute guarantee against falls. It describes a controller approach, not an established outcome.
Does the Bayesian estimate dictate the next foot placement?

The proposal connects estimation and planning, but it does not specify a rule that maps an estimate to a particular placement. The estimate can inform how the controller reasons about uncertain support, while viability-constrained MPC reserves recovery steps. A precise placement rule is not stated.
Are the graded probes and the recovery reservation competing goals?

They address a tension within the same proposal. Graded-load probes seek information about an unknown yield limit; reserving recovery steps keeps that exploration from consuming all planned recovery options. The statement does not specify a numerical trade-off or an optimization weight between them.
Would it be accurate to say that Bayesian inference replaces the need for recovery planning?

No. An uncertain estimate of a yield limit is not itself a recovery plan. The proposal explicitly includes both Bayesian force–sinkage inference and viability-constrained MPC that reserves recovery steps, so neither component should be presented as a substitute for the other.
Does this commit us to a particular terrain material or sensing package?

No terrain material or sensing package is specified. The proposed inference uses force–sinkage information from graded-load foot probes, but the statement does not say how those quantities are sensed or restrict the approach to a named substrate.
How should I explain the proposal in one sentence without claiming it already works?

Propose using graded-load foot probes and Bayesian force–sinkage inference to estimate hidden terrain yield limits, while viability-constrained MPC reserves recovery steps during exploration. That states the intended approach without presenting its performance as an observed result.
Can graded foot probes identify yield load without shrinking the viability-constrained MPC recovery set below a safe margin?

That is the central open question for this approach. Graded probes are intended to reveal the terrain’s yield load, but each exploratory contact must also leave the viability-constrained MPC with enough recovery options. The question asks whether both can hold at once; it does not establish that they can.
What exactly is in tension?

Learning the yield load may call for applying informative loads through the foot. At the same time, a probe must not leave the controller with a recovery set smaller than the safe margin. The tension is between gaining information from contact and preserving room to recover if the terrain’s support is uncertain.
When you say “recovery set,” are you referring to the recovery steps the MPC reserves?

Yes, in the sense of the recovery possibilities the viability-constrained MPC is meant to keep available. The question asks whether graded probing can preserve a sufficiently large set of those possibilities. It does not define the set mathematically or specify which recovery steps it contains.
Does “safe margin” give us a numerical threshold?

No. It says the recovery set must not shrink below a safe margin, but it does not assign that margin a value or state how it is measured. We can preserve that requirement without inventing a threshold.
Could we answer yes just because MPC is viability-constrained?

No. Calling the MPC viability-constrained describes the intended planning safeguard; it does not, by itself, show that the probes will be informative enough to identify yield load while the recovery set stays above the safe margin. That coexistence is precisely what the question leaves open.
Could we answer no because an informative probe must always use up too much recoverability?

That would also go beyond what is stated. The question raises a possible conflict, but it does not establish that every informative probe reduces the recovery set below the margin. Whether adequate information and adequate recoverability can coexist remains unresolved here.
Is the question only about avoiding an immediate fall during a probe?

It is more specific than that. It asks whether the controller can identify yield load *without shrinking the viability-constrained MPC recovery set below a safe margin*. Avoiding an immediate fall would not, on its own, answer whether sufficient recovery options remain available.
If a probe gives useful force–sinkage information but leaves too few recovery options, does it meet the condition?
No. Useful information addresses the identification side, but the question also requires the recovery set not to fall below the safe margin. Both conditions have to be considered together.
What if the recovery set stays comfortably large but the probes never identify the yield load?

That would satisfy only the recoverability side. The question is whether *graded foot probes can identify yield load* while preserving the stipulated recovery margin, not merely whether probing can be kept conservative.
Does the question require the yield load to be observed directly?

It does not say so. “Identify yield load” can be read alongside the proposed force–sinkage inference: the issue is whether information from graded probes can support identification without sacrificing the required recovery margin. The question does not prescribe a direct observation or a particular inference criterion.
Should we assume the same probe intensity will work on every previously unseen terrain?

No such assumption is supplied. The question does not specify probe intensities or claim that one loading pattern works across terrains. Its focus is the compatibility of identifying yield load and keeping the MPC recovery set above a safe margin.
Can you restate the question without turning it into a claim of success?

Can graded-load foot probing provide enough information to identify the terrain’s yield load while viability-constrained MPC retains a recovery set that does not drop below a safe margin? That keeps both requirements explicit and leaves the answer open.
What hypothesis would address whether graded foot probes can identify yield load while preserving a safe recovery margin?

The hypothesis is that viability-gated probes maintain a recovery-step margin of at least 0.15 m while estimating yield load with a median relative error below 15%. It proposes that probing can meet both the recoverability and estimation conditions; it is not a reported result.
What does “viability-gated” add to the probe idea?

It makes continued recoverability a condition on exploratory probing. The probes are not considered solely for the information they might provide about yield load; they must also be compatible with preserving the recovery-step margin. The hypothesis does not specify the gate’s exact calculation or decision rule.
Is the 0.15 m figure a target for how far the robot should step after every probe?

No. It is a lower bound on the *recovery-step margin* in the hypothesis, not a prescribed step length or an instruction to take a recovery step after each probe. The statement does not define how that margin is computed.
So what do the two inequalities mean exactly?

The recovery-step margin is hypothesized to remain **at least 0.15 m**, so equality with 0.15 m meets that bound. The median relative error in estimating yield load is hypothesized to be **below 15%**, so an error equal to 15% would not meet that bound.
Does the error threshold mean every yield-load estimate has to be within 15%?
No. The hypothesis specifies *median* relative error below 15%, not an error below 15% for every estimate. It also does not provide an evaluation set or a detailed method for calculating the errors.
Could an estimate satisfy the accuracy part even if a probe leaves less than 0.15 m of recovery-step margin?

It could satisfy the accuracy condition considered alone, but it would not satisfy the full hypothesis. The claim joins the two conditions: viability-gated probes are hypothesized to preserve a recovery-step margin of at least 0.15 m *while* estimating yield load with median relative error below 15%.
And if the margin stays at 0.15 m or more but the median error is 15%?
Then the stated error condition would not be met. The margin condition permits 0.15 m exactly; the accuracy condition requires a value strictly less than 15%.
Does this hypothesis say that a probe must discover the exact yielding point?

No. It concerns estimating yield load to a specified median relative-error threshold. It does not require an exact estimate from any individual probe or prescribe that the terrain be pushed to its yielding point.
How does it relate to the question about the viability-constrained MPC recovery set?

It gives that question a concrete, testable form: can probing identify yield load to the stated accuracy while retaining a recovery-step margin of at least 0.15 m? The margin expresses the recoverability side of the hypothesis. It does not, by itself, define the entire MPC recovery set or establish that the hypothesis is true.
Can I call 0.15 m a proven safe margin?
No. The hypothesis names 0.15 m as its proposed minimum recovery-step margin. It does not report evidence that this value is sufficient for safety or that the probes have maintained it.
Is the margin threshold the same thing as the 15% estimation threshold?

No. They describe different quantities with different units and inequality directions. The recovery-step margin is a distance and must be at least 0.15 m; the estimation criterion is a median relative error and must be below 15%. One cannot substitute for the other.
Would it be accurate to say the viability gate guarantees both thresholds?

That would present a hypothesis as a guarantee. The proposed claim is that viability-gated probes *would* maintain the ≥0.15 m recovery-step margin while achieving <15% median relative error in yield-load estimates. Whether they do so remains to be established.
Does the hypothesis specify when or how often the margin is checked?

No checking schedule is specified. “Maintain” expresses the intended preservation of the recovery-step margin during probing, but the hypothesis does not state a sampling frequency, calculation procedure, or particular gate implementation.
Could I summarize it as trading away some recovery room for a better estimate?

Only with care. The hypothesis allows for probing while requiring that the recovery-step margin remain at least 0.15 m. It does not quantify any amount of recovery room spent or assert a particular trade-off between margin and estimation accuracy.
Please give me the hypothesis in one precise sentence.
The hypothesis is that viability-gated foot probes can estimate yield load with median relative error below 15% while maintaining a recovery-step margin of at least 0.15 m.
How would we evaluate the viability-gated probe hypothesis?

The proposed evaluation is to use 300 blinded terrain trials and measure three outcomes: plate-referenced median yield error, the minimum recovery-step margin, and matched-speed fall reduction. Together, those measurements address estimation, retained recoverability, and falls during traversal. This is an evaluation activity, not a report that the trials have been run.
Is 300 the number of probes or the number of terrain trials?
It is the number of blinded terrain trials. The activity does not state how many foot probes occur within any trial.
What should I take “blinded” to mean here?

It characterizes the 300 terrain trials as blinded. The activity does not specify who or what is blinded, or the procedure used to maintain blinding, so those details should not be filled in as though they were already decided.
What is the purpose of the plate reference in the yield-error measurement?

It provides the stated reference against which the yield-load estimate is assessed. “Plate-referenced median yield error” says what the error is referenced to and that the reported error is a median; it does not specify the plate procedure or an exact error formula.
Are we reporting the error from the best-looking terrain trial?
No. The activity calls for a median yield error across the blinded terrain trials, referenced to the plate measurement. Selecting a best-looking trial would not be the same measurement.
Why record the minimum recovery-step margin rather than just saying the controller planned recovery steps?

Planning recovery steps alone would not say how much margin remained. Recording the minimum recovery-step margin makes the smallest observed margin part of the evaluation, so the recoverability claim can be examined alongside the yield estimate. The activity does not specify the exact calculation or reporting procedure for that minimum.
Could we substitute an average recovery-step margin for the minimum?
Not without changing the activity. It explicitly calls for the *minimum* recovery-step margin. An average could obscure a smaller margin, and it is not the stated measurement.
What does “matched-speed fall reduction” require us to keep in view?

The fall comparison must be made at equal traversal speed. In the stated goal, the comparator is an otherwise matched nonexploratory controller. The activity calls for measuring the reduction in falls under that matched-speed comparison; it does not provide a fall count or a measured reduction.
If the exploratory controller travels more slowly, can we still call a lower fall count the matched-speed reduction?
Not on that basis. A fall comparison made at different traversal speeds would not satisfy the activity’s matched-speed condition, even if one controller had fewer falls.
Does this activity already tell us whether the accuracy and recovery-margin targets have been met?

No. It identifies what to measure on the 300 blinded terrain trials. It supplies no observed plate-referenced median yield error, minimum recovery-step margin, or matched-speed fall reduction, so it cannot establish whether the targets are met.
Can the three measurements be treated as interchangeable signs of success?

No. Each addresses a different aspect of the controller: yield error concerns estimation against the plate reference; minimum recovery-step margin concerns retained recovery room; and matched-speed fall reduction concerns falls relative to the comparator. Measuring one does not supply the value of another.
Does the activity say how the 300 trials are divided between controllers or terrain conditions?
It does not. The specified count is 300 blinded terrain trials, and the specified outcomes include a matched-speed fall reduction. No allocation of trials or list of terrain conditions is given.
Give me a faithful description of the evaluation without inventing a protocol.

On 300 blinded terrain trials, measure plate-referenced median yield error, minimum recovery-step margin, and fall reduction versus an otherwise matched nonexploratory controller at equal traversal speed. The trial allocation, blinding procedure, plate procedure, and resulting values are not specified.
What were the measurements from the blinded terrain trials?

In 300 blinded trials, the plate-referenced median yield error was 12.8%, the minimum recovery-step margin was 0.16 m, and matched-speed falls were 12 versus 18. Those are the reported observations; the figures do not specify results for individual trials.
Which controller had 12 falls?

In the stated comparison, the exploratory controller had 12 falls versus 18 for the otherwise matched nonexploratory controller, with traversal speed equal. The counts should be kept together with that matched-speed condition.
What is the numerical difference between the fall counts?

There were six fewer falls in the 12-fall count than in the 18-fall count. Relative to 18, that difference is one-third, or about 33.3%. That calculation describes the reported counts; it does not add information about how the trials were allocated.
Does the 12.8% figure describe every yield-load estimate?

No. It is a *median* yield error. Individual errors could differ; the evidence gives neither their distribution nor the error from any particular trial. The error was reported with reference to the plate measurement.
What should I understand from the 0.16 m figure?

It is the reported *minimum* recovery-step margin, expressed as a distance. It is not an average margin or a prescribed length for a recovery step. The evidence does not give the margins at other points in the trials.
Can I say the margin was exactly 0.16 m throughout all 300 trials?
No. A reported minimum of 0.16 m does not mean the margin was constant. It identifies the smallest margin reported in the evaluation, without describing how the margin varied.
Do the 300 blinded trials tell us how many probes were made?
No. The count is for blinded terrain trials, not foot probes. The evidence does not say how many probes occurred within or across those trials.
Do we know from these figures which terrain was hardest to estimate?
No. The median yield error summarizes the reported errors, but there is no terrain-by-terrain breakdown or identification of a hardest terrain.
Is the fall result a comparison at whatever speeds the two controllers happened to achieve?
No. The falls are reported as a *matched-speed* comparison: 12 versus 18 at equal traversal speed. The evidence does not give the speed itself.
Would it be accurate to report only that falls decreased, leaving out the counts?

That would lose useful precision. The reported evidence is 12 versus 18 matched-speed falls. Giving both counts makes the size and basis of the comparison clear without implying an unreported trial-by-trial pattern.
Can these measurements tell us that every exploratory contact remained recoverable?

They do not establish that statement about every contact. The evidence reports a minimum recovery-step margin of 0.16 m and aggregate fall counts, but it does not provide a contact-by-contact account or an absolute guarantee of recoverability.
Please state the evidence plainly, without adding an interpretation of the earlier targets.

Across 300 blinded terrain trials, plate-referenced median yield error was 12.8%, minimum recovery-step margin was 0.16 m, and matched-speed falls numbered 12 for the exploratory controller versus 18 for the otherwise matched nonexploratory controller.
What decision follows from the blinded trials?
Advance viability-gated probing to hardware validation. The stated reason is that the blinded trials met the estimation and recovery thresholds and cut matched-speed falls by 33%.
Does “advance to hardware validation” mean the controller has already been validated on hardware?
No. It is a decision to move viability-gated probing into hardware validation, not a report of completed hardware validation or its outcome.
What exactly supports making that move?

The decision rests on the blinded-trial results: the estimation threshold was met, the recovery threshold was met, and matched-speed falls were reduced by 33%. Those are the reasons given for advancing; the decision does not rely on an unstated hardware result.
Is the 33% figure an overall reduction in all failures?
No. It refers specifically to falls in the matched-speed comparison. It should not be broadened to all failures or described without the equal-traversal-speed condition.
What is the comparison behind “matched-speed falls”?

It is the comparison with an otherwise matched nonexploratory controller at equal traversal speed. The decision reports a 33% fall reduction under that comparison, not a reduction inferred from controllers moving at different speeds.
Could I say the blinded trials prove viability-gated probing will be safe on hardware?

That would go beyond the decision. The blinded trials are the stated basis for proceeding to hardware validation; they do not establish what the hardware-validation results will be or provide an absolute safety guarantee.
Is this an instruction to deploy the controller in ordinary operation?
No. The specified next stage is hardware validation. Deployment or routine use is not part of this decision.
Do we need to choose a new probe method before advancing?
The decision names viability-gated probing as what advances. It does not specify a replacement method or a change to the probing approach.
Does meeting the recovery threshold mean every possible recovery maneuver is guaranteed?
No. The decision says the blinded trials met the recovery threshold. It does not make a claim about every possible maneuver or guarantee recoverability under all hardware conditions.
How should I describe the role of the estimation result without overstating it?

Say that meeting the estimation threshold was one reason for advancing viability-gated probing to hardware validation. Avoid turning that into a claim that yield-load estimates are exact or that their accuracy has already been established on hardware.
What if I describe the decision as based only on the fall reduction?
That would omit part of its stated rationale. The decision depends on the blinded trials meeting both the estimation and recovery thresholds *and* cutting matched-speed falls by 33%.
Conversely, would meeting the estimation and recovery thresholds alone capture the full reason?
No. The matched-speed fall reduction is also expressly part of the reason. All three elements belong in a faithful account of the decision.
Does the decision prescribe the hardware-validation procedure?
No. It identifies hardware validation as the next stage for viability-gated probing, but gives no hardware platform, test sequence, acceptance criterion, or schedule.
Can I phrase this as a finding that hardware validation will succeed?
No. The decision is to *advance to* hardware validation because of the blinded-trial findings. Whether hardware validation succeeds remains unreported here.
Give me a precise statement I can use.
Advance viability-gated probing to hardware validation because the blinded trials met the estimation and recovery thresholds and reduced falls by 33% in a matched-speed comparison.
What is the hardware-validation plan for viability-gated probing?

Run 120 randomized hardware traversals on unseen yielding beds. Compare matched-speed falls, plate-referenced yield error, and recovery margin against the baseline. This specifies what to test and compare; it does not report hardware results.
Are there 120 traversals for each controller?

The plan says 120 randomized hardware traversals in total. It does not specify how those traversals are allocated between the controller and the baseline, so I would not describe the count as 120 per controller.
What does “randomized” commit us to?

It commits the plan to randomized traversals, but does not specify what is randomized or how. An allocation procedure, terrain order, or other randomization detail would need to be stated separately rather than assumed.
Why specify hardware traversals rather than just more terrain trials?

The plan specifically calls for testing during hardware traversals on unseen yielding beds. That identifies the setting for these comparisons without asserting that any hardware traversal has already occurred or specifying the hardware platform.
What counts as an “unseen yielding bed” in this description?

It is a yielding terrain bed that is unseen for the evaluation in the sense relevant to the plan. The wording does not name a material, set a yielding limit, or specify how unfamiliarity is established. Those details should not be supplied as if they were already in the plan.
Is the baseline the otherwise matched nonexploratory controller?
That is the comparator identified for the legged-locomotion goal, so it provides the relevant meaning of “baseline” here. The plan does not give further baseline implementation details.
Which of the comparisons explicitly requires equal traversal speed?

The fall comparison is explicitly a matched-speed comparison. Falls should therefore be compared at equal traversal speed rather than credited to one controller while it travels more slowly. The plan also calls for comparing plate-referenced yield error and recovery margin against the baseline, without spelling out additional matching conditions for those measures.
What are we comparing when we say “plate-referenced yield error”?

We are comparing yield-load estimation error with a plate reference as the stated point of reference. The plan calls for that error to be compared against the baseline. It does not describe the plate measurement procedure or the exact error calculation.
Does this plan specifically say to report the median yield error?

It says to compare plate-referenced yield error, but does not specify an aggregate such as a median in the hardware plan itself. The broader estimation goal uses median relative error below 15%; that does not supply an unspoken reporting procedure for these 120 traversals.
Could I say the plan will show whether every individual estimate is within 15%?

No. The hardware plan does not state an individual-estimate threshold, and the broader 15% target concerns a median relative error, not every estimate. The plan names an error measurement and comparison, not an outcome for each traversal.
What does comparing recovery margin against the baseline contribute?

It makes retained recovery room an explicit comparison, alongside estimation error and falls. That matters because the controller is meant to explore yielding support while maintaining recoverability. The plan does not specify a recovery-margin formula or report a hardware margin.
Does it say the hardware comparison uses the minimum recovery margin?

No. The hardware plan says “recovery margin” without specifying whether the comparison uses a minimum, an average, or another summary. Calling it a minimum here would add a detail that this plan does not state.
Will every traversal necessarily include an exploratory foot probe?

The plan is for hardware validation of the probing approach, but it does not specify the number or timing of exploratory contacts within a traversal. It would be unwarranted to assert a probe count for each run.
Does comparing yield error against a nonexploratory baseline tell us how that baseline generates a yield estimate?
No. The plan calls for the comparison but does not explain how the baseline’s yield error is obtained. We can state the intended comparison without inventing an estimation mechanism for the baseline.
If the two controllers produce different numbers of falls, can we ignore traversal speed?
No. The plan explicitly calls for *matched-speed* falls. A raw difference in fall counts at unequal traversal speeds would not, on its own, be the specified fall comparison.
Does the plan already establish that falls will decrease on hardware?
No. It proposes measuring and comparing hardware falls. It does not provide hardware fall counts, a reduction percentage, or a conclusion about which controller will fall less.
What if the plate-referenced error looks good but the recovery margin is small?

The plan requires looking at both measures; favorable yield error alone would not describe the recovery-margin comparison. It does not specify how to judge a particular hardware margin or make a decision from a mixed result.
And if recovery margin is large but falls are not lower at matched speed?

That would still call for reporting the matched-speed fall comparison separately. A recovery-margin measurement cannot stand in for a fall outcome. The plan does not prescribe a decision rule for any such combination of results.
Can we specify a particular bed material, traverse length, or robot configuration when presenting this plan?

Not as facts supplied by the plan. It specifies 120 randomized hardware traversals on unseen yielding beds and names three comparisons against the baseline. It does not specify bed materials, traverse lengths, or a robot configuration.
What is the shortest faithful statement of the plan?
Run 120 randomized hardware traversals on unseen yielding beds, comparing matched-speed falls, plate-referenced yield error, and recovery margin against the otherwise matched nonexploratory baseline.
What does the hardware-traversal activity call for?

Run 60 matched-speed hardware traversals per controller on blinded yielding beds. During those traversals, log plate-referenced yield error, falls, and recovery margin. This describes the activity and what it records, not its results.
How many traversals is that altogether?
With two controllers in the comparison and 60 traversals per controller, that is 120 hardware traversals in total. The activity does not say how many distinct yielding beds those traversals cover.
Which two controllers are being compared?

The comparison concerns the viability-gated probing controller and the otherwise matched nonexploratory baseline. The activity specifies 60 matched-speed traversals per controller; it does not add implementation details for either one.
Does “per controller” mean 60 runs of the probing controller and 60 of the baseline, rather than 60 shared between them?
Yes. The count is 60 for each controller, not 60 divided between them.
What does matched-speed require of the fall comparison?

The controllers’ falls must be compared at equal traversal speed. A lower fall count obtained by moving more slowly would not, by itself, be the matched-speed comparison specified here. No numerical traversal speed is given.
Does matched-speed tell us that every pair of traversals uses exactly the same bed?
No. It specifies speed matching, not a bed-pairing procedure. The activity says the traversals are on blinded yielding beds but does not say whether or how individual traversals are paired by bed.
What is meant by blinded yielding beds?

The activity characterizes the yielding beds as blinded, but it does not spell out the blinding procedure or who lacks which information. It also does not name the bed materials or their yielding limits.
Are these simulations with hardware-like parameters?
No—the specified activity is to run *hardware traversals*. It does not identify a particular robot or hardware setup, but replacing the runs with simulations would change what the activity calls for.
What exactly gets logged during each traversal?
The named records are plate-referenced yield error, falls, and recovery margin. The activity does not prescribe a logging frequency, a data format, or an aggregation method for those records.
What does “plate-referenced” qualify?
It qualifies the yield-error measurement: the error is assessed relative to a plate reference. The activity does not describe the plate procedure or give a formula for computing the error.
Should I say we record the estimated yield load but not its error?

That would miss the stated measure. The activity specifically calls for logging *plate-referenced yield error*. It does not separately specify which underlying estimates or reference readings are retained.
Does “falls” mean we log only a final fall percentage?

No final percentage is specified. The activity says to log falls during the traversals. A later comparison could use those records, but no fall count, percentage, or reduction is reported in this activity.
Does “recovery margin” mean the minimum margin across all runs?
